contenido: 1. The doctrine and use of indulgences, in force in the Catholic Church for many centuries, are solidly based on divine revelation, which, bequeathed by the Apostles, "progresses in the Church with the assistance of the Holy Spirit", while "the Church, in the course of the centuries, constantly tends towards the fullness of divine truth, until the words of God are fulfilled in it."

2. As divine revelation teaches us, punishments are a consequence of sins, inflicted by divine holiness and justice, and must be purged either in this world, with the pains, miseries and sadness of this life and especially with death, or by means of fire, torments and catharteria punishments in the future life. For this reason, the faithful were always convinced that the evil path had many difficulties and that it was rough, thorny and harmful to those who walked along it.

3. Therefore, it is necessary for the full remission and reparation of sins not only to restore friendship with God through a sincere conversion of the mind, and to expiate the offense inflicted on his wisdom and goodness, but also to fully restore all personal, social and those related to the universal order, destroyed or disturbed by sin, either through voluntary reparation, which will not be without sacrifice, or through the acceptance of the penalties established by the just and holy divine wisdom, so that the holiness and splendor of the glory of God may shine throughout the world. The folly and malice of sin, and its bad consequences, are deduced from the existence and severity of the penalties.

4. By arcane and merciful designs of God, men are linked to each other by supernatural ties, so that the sin of one harms others, in the same way that the holiness of one benefits others. In this way, the faithful provide mutual help to achieve the supernatural goal. A testimony of this communion is already manifested in Adam, whose sin spread to all men. But the greatest and most perfect principle, foundation and example of this supernatural bond is Christ himself, to whose union with him God has called us.
5. For Christ, who "committed no sin," "suffered his passion for us"; "He was pierced by our rebellions, crushed by our crimes..., and his scars healed us."

6. The Church, aware from the beginning of these truths, began various paths to apply to each faithful the fruits of Christ's redemption, and so that the faithful would strive for the salvation of their brothers; and so that in this way the entire body of the Church would be built in justice and holiness for the coming of the kingdom of God, when God will be all in all. The Apostles themselves exhorted their disciples to pray for the salvation of sinners; A very ancient custom of the Church has preserved this way of doing things, especially when the penitents begged the intercession of the entire community, and the deceased were helped with suffrages, especially with the offering of the Eucharistic sacrifice. Also good works, especially those most difficult for human frailty, were offered to God in ancient times in the Church for the salvation of sinners. Since the sufferings that the martyrs endured through faith and the law of God were greatly esteemed, the penitents used to pray to them, so that, helped by their merits, they could more quickly achieve reconciliation on the part of the Bishops. For the prayers and good works of the righteous were so valued that it was certain that the penitent would be washed, clean and redeemed with the help of all the Christian people.

7. The current persuasion in the Church that the shepherds of the Lord's flock could free the faithful from the relics of sins by the application of the merits of Christ and the saints, little by little, throughout the centuries, by inspiration of the Holy Spirit, soul of the people of God, suggested the use of indulgences, by means of which progress was made in this same doctrine and discipline of the Church; It was a progress and not a change, and a new good drawn from the root of revelation for the benefit of the faithful and the entire Church.
8. This remission of the temporal punishment due for sins, already forgiven as far as guilt is concerned, was designated by the name "indulgence."
9. Today the Church also invites all her children to meditate and consider the great value of the use of indulgences for individual life and for the promotion of Christian society.

10. Furthermore, indulgences increase confidence and hope for full reconciliation with God the Father, giving no respite from abandonment or allowing the cultivation of the dispositions required for full communion with God to be neglected. For indulgences, despite being free benefits, are only granted, both to the living and the deceased, once certain conditions have been met, requiring to earn them either that the prescribed good works have been carried out, or that the faithful be endowed with the proper dispositions, that is, that they love God, detest sins, have confidence in the merits of Christ and firmly believe that the communion of saints is of great use to them.

11. Based on these truths, Holy Mother Church, in once again recommending to the faithful the use of indulgences, as a use very pleasing to the Christian people throughout many centuries and also in our times, as experience proves, does not intend to downplay the other forms of sanctification and purification, especially the holy sacrifice of the mass and the sacraments, especially the sacrament of penance, nor the copious aids called under the common name of sacramentals, nor to works of piety, penance and charity. All these forms have in common that sanctification and purification operate with all the more validity the more closely one is united to Christ, the head, and to the body of the Church, through charity. Indulgences also confirm the supremacy of charity in the Christian life. For they cannot be gained without a sincere metanoia and union with God, to which is added the fulfillment of the prescribed works. The order of charity, therefore, remains in place, in which the remission of penalties is inserted by dispensation of the treasury of the Church.
12. The norms that follow introduce the appropriate variations in the discipline of indulgences, having taken into account the wishes of the Episcopal Conferences.
